Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

We continue with module one on molecular spectroscopy and in today's class we are going to derive the expression for rotational energy levels of a diatomic molecule.

Key details

  • We will study the selection rules and finally we will arrive at the rotational spectrum.
  • We need a model in order to understand how the molecule is going to behave, and we can see here what we are going to use is a rigid rotor molecule.
  • We have two atoms heteronuclear so the masses are different and they are held together by a rigid rod and that is having a center of gravity at the point C.
  • which are held together by a rigid rod, meaning that whenever there is rotation, this rod will not change its form.
  • Now we have masses M1 and M2 which are joined by a thin rod, so therefore R0 is going to be R1 plus R2.
  • Therefore, we can write the balancing equation m1r1 is equal to m2r2.
  • M2 R2 R1 plus M1 R1 R2.
  • All we have done is replaced M1 R1 by M2 R2 and here M2 R2 by M1 R1.
  • And what we get is I is equal to R1 R2 M1 plus M two.
  • Because there is a rotation which is happening.
  • Now since m1 r one is equal to m2 r2 we can also write this as m2 r naught minus r1 because we said that r naught is equal to r one plus r2.
  • And why do we require this?
  • Because we want to substitute R1 here.
  • So therefore R2 is equal to M1 R0 by M1 plus M2.
  • When we substitute for R1 and R2 in this expression for moment of inertia we get this expression i is equal to m1 m2 divided by m1 plus m2 r naught square which can be written as mu r naught square.

Example or application from the lecture

  • So let us get to the expressions of rotational energy levels for a diatomic molecule, because that is the simplest molecule.
  • So let us take the case of a diatomic molecule and heteronuclear diatomic molecule of course because homonuclear diatomic molecules will not be microwave active.
  • Let us see how the derivation goes.
